lesson.title: Making It Happen: Calling a Function
lesson.summary: A function call, the function's name followed by parentheses, is what actually triggers the code inside a function to run, using whatever values you place inside those parentheses.
lesson.body:
Defining a function with def only creates it, ready and waiting. Nothing inside the function body runs until you write a function call: the function's name followed by parentheses, as in square(5). The moment Python evaluates that expression, it does something quite different from evaluating an ordinary expression like 5 + 3. Execution jumps out of wherever the call appears and into the top of the function's body, runs the statements there in order using whatever values were passed in, and then jumps back to exactly the spot the call happened, carrying along whatever the function returned.

This jump-and-return behavior is worth tracing carefully, because it is easy to describe but subtle to watch happen. Suppose you have def square(n): return n * n defined earlier, and then your program runs:

print("Before")
result = square(5)
print("After:", result)

Execution starts at print("Before"), which runs immediately and prints Before. Next, Python begins evaluating square(5). This is where the jump happens: control transfers into square's body with n bound to 5, the statement return n * n computes 5 * 5, which is 25, and the function hands 25 back to the exact spot the call was made, which is the right-hand side of result = square(5). So result is assigned 25, and only then does the program move to the next line, print("After:", result), which prints After: 25. Notice the order: the body of square ran entirely between the two print statements, even though square does not appear anywhere near them in the source code, because a call redirects control to wherever the function was defined, not wherever it happens to sit visually in the file.

A function can be called as many times as you like once it is defined, and each call is independent. square(5) followed later by square(9) does not remember anything from the first call; each call starts fresh with whatever value is passed that time, computing 25 and then 81 with no interaction between them. This is what makes a single definition reusable across an entire program: the def statement is written once, but the call can appear dozens of times, in different places, with different values, and every one of those calls triggers its own independent run through the same body.

It also matters that a function call is an expression, meaning it produces a value and can be used anywhere a value is allowed, not just on its own line. You can write print(square(4)), where square(4) is evaluated first, producing 16, and that 16 is then what actually gets passed to print. You can write square(3) + square(4), which calls square twice, getting 9 and 16, and adds them to get 25. This ability to nest calls inside larger expressions is exactly what makes functions composable: once square is defined, it behaves like any other value-producing piece of Python, plugging directly into arithmetic, into other function calls, or into conditions, rather than being some separate, special kind of statement.
